1.title: Know the handy trade
1.intro: Handy workers fix and improve homes: small repairs, fitting, painting, assembly. Know the limits of your trade first.
pts: Name common jobs: patching walls, painting, shelves, door and tap repairs, furniture assembly.
Describe which jobs need a licensed trade, such as electrical, gas and some plumbing.
Name the basic tools: tape measure, level, drill, screwdrivers, stud finder.
List words: stud, anchor, caulk, primer, torque, shut-off valve.
Classify a job as handy, licensed trade or refer on, and write the reason.
Compare a small repair with a renovation and say where your limit sits.
Identify signs of a larger problem, such as mould, a sagging floor or repeated leaks.
1.ex: A customer asks for a new light fitting and a leaking shower. Light wiring may need a licensed electrician; a loose tap washer may be fine for a handy worker. The worker splits the request into two jobs and writes which one is referred on.
1.act: List ten common jobs and mark each: handy worker, or licensed trade needed (check locally).
1.std: Task: sort jobs by scope. Condition: ten example jobs. Standard: each job marked with a reason and checked with the local authority.

2.title: Work safely
2.intro: Tools, ladders and dust can hurt. Safety comes before speed.
pts: Apply tool safety: eye cover, gloves, hearing cover, dust mask where needed.
Use ladders correctly: firm base, three points of contact, do not overreach.
Check for hidden hazards before cutting or drilling: pipes, wires, old paint or insulation.
Explain why you stop and ask when you suspect something dangerous.
Wear a dust mask that suits the dust and check that it seals on the face.
Secure the work area with tape and signs, and keep cords out of walking paths.
Lift with the legs, ask for help with heavy items and use a trolley.
2.ex: Before drilling into a wall, the worker uses a detector, checks the other side, then drills a small pilot hole. Old paint in an old house is tested before sanding. To reach a point 4 m up, a ladder base sits about 1 m out from the wall (the one-in-four rule).
2.act: Write a safety checklist for ladder, drill and paint jobs and use it on a practice job.
2.std: Task: do a safe set-up. Condition: practice job. Standard: every checklist item done before work starts.

3.title: Follow the rules in Canada
3.intro: Trades licensing, permits, insurance and tax rules differ by province. Check with the local authority.
pts: Explain that electrical, gas and many plumbing jobs need a licensed person; check your province.
Describe building permits: some work needs one; ask the city before you start.
Check insurance and compensation rules for working alone or hiring helpers.
Apply tax and contract rules: written quote, receipts, and sales tax rules checked with the federal tax agency.
Identify the city office to call for permit questions and write down the contact.
Describe when a landlord or condo board must approve work.
Keep a copy of the quote, permit and insurance for every job.
3.ex: Rules table row: Permit | city building office | ask before structural or electrical changes | before work | permit number in job file. A second row: Landlord approval | building owner | ask in writing before changes to walls or fixtures | before work | reply kept. Add a checked date to each row.
3.act: Make a rules table for your city and province with official pages and dates.
3.std: Task: map the rules. Condition: official pages only. Standard: each row has an enforcer, an action and a checked date.

4.title: Do core repairs to a standard
4.intro: Learn a few repairs well rather than many badly.
pts: Build a method for a wall patch: clean, fill, dry, sand, prime, paint.
Apply a method for hanging a shelf: find studs, level, right anchors, load check.
Fix a dripping tap or running toilet by following the manufacturer steps.
Record before and after photos.
Sequence a repair in steps and write the tools and materials list before starting.
Check a finished repair with a level, a tug test or a water test.
Clean and put away tools, then note what to improve.
4.ex: Shelf job: stud found, level marked, two screws into the stud, anchor in one spot, load test, photo taken. If the shelf will hold three book sets of 2 kg and a 4 kg box, the planned load is 3 x 2 + 4 = 10 kg, and the load test uses that weight.
4.act: Do each of three repairs twice on a practice board and compare the second run.
4.std: Task: complete a repair. Condition: practice board. Standard: result level, firm and clean, and the second run is better.

5.title: Read the problem and quote
5.intro: Many handy jobs fail because the real problem was missed. Look first, then quote.
pts: Ask questions: what, where, since when, what was tried.
Check the cause, not just the sign. A stain on a ceiling may come from above.
Write a quote with scope, materials, time, price and what is not included.
Explain a change order and why it must be agreed before extra work.
Take photos and measurements at the first visit.
Decide when to say 'I must look closer' instead of guessing a price.
Explain an allowance for hidden problems, such as extra time for an old house.
5.ex: Ceiling stain: the leak is from the bathroom above. The quote covers finding the cause (1 hour); painting is a second step after it is dry (3 hours). The two steps total 4 hours, and the client approves each one.
5.act: Visit two practice jobs, write the problem, cause and a written quote.
5.std: Task: quote a job. Condition: practice site. Standard: scope, materials, price and exclusions all written.

6.title: Price, materials and time
6.intro: Time and materials add up fast. Count the trip to the store too.
pts: Compute job cost: labour, materials with a small mark-up, travel, tools wear, insurance.
Compare hourly and fixed prices.
Plan the day with buffer time for surprises.
Check supplier prices at three stores before buying.
Calculate materials with waste: add about 10% for cuts, then round up to whole packs.
Compute the mark-up on materials and tell the client.
Track real time against quoted time to improve the next quote.
6.ex: Price 120 for a 2-hour job, materials 15, travel 10. Margin = 120 - 15 - 10 = 95. If fixed costs are 600 a month, break-even is 600 / 95 = 6.3, so 7 jobs (teaching numbers only).
6.act: Build a cost sheet and a price list for five common jobs.
6.std: Task: price jobs. Condition: all costs counted. Standard: margin and break-even correct and shown with units.

7.title: Clients, trust and records
7.intro: You work in people's homes. Respect, tidiness and honesty bring referrals.
pts: Apply site care: cover floors, clean up, take away waste.
Write a short agreement: scope, price, timing, payment, warranty on your work.
Keep a job file: quote, photos, receipts, notes.
Handle a mistake: say it, fix it, record it.
Take photos only with permission and never share the inside of a home.
Explain your warranty in plain words: its length and what is not covered.
Ask for payment on the date agreed and issue a receipt.
7.ex: Paint drips on a floor. The worker tells the client, cleans it at once and writes a note. The client keeps using the service, and the note goes in the job file.
7.act: Create a job file template and run one practice job through it from quote to final photo.
7.std: Task: finish a job properly. Condition: practice job. Standard: site clean, file complete and client signs off.

8.title: Run the service for real
8.intro: Now run your handy service with real clients, a plan and clear limits.
pts: Run a 60-day pilot with a stop rule agreed in advance.
Review weekly: jobs, margin, repeat jobs, complaints, referrals.
Create a 12-month plan with training, insurance and tools.
Lead others: write job methods so a helper can do the same standard.
Calculate the share of quotes that become jobs.
Set a rule to decline jobs outside your skills or insurance.
Cost the tools and training in the 12-month plan and decide which to buy first.
8.ex: Stop rule: if fewer than 15 jobs in 60 days, stop and write lessons. Result: 22 jobs and 6 referrals, so 6 / 22 = about 27% of jobs came from referrals. 22 is above 15, so the pilot continues and shelf-and-assembly packages are added.
8.act: Run the pilot, write the review and present your plan to three people.
8.std: Task: run a handy service pilot. Condition: 60 days, real clients. Standard: results compared with the stop rule and trade limits re-checked.

quiz: Name two jobs that may need a licensed trade.
Electrical and gas (also some plumbing); check locally.
What do you do before drilling a wall?
Check for pipes and wires with a detector and plan the hole.
What are three points of contact on a ladder?
Two hands and one foot, or two feet and one hand, always touching.
Why ask the city about permits?
Some work needs a permit and doing it without one can cause trouble.
What should a quote include?
Scope, materials, time, price and what is not included.
What is a change order?
An agreed written change to scope or price before extra work.
Why find the cause, not just the sign?
The stain or drip may come from another place.
How do you find break-even jobs?
Fixed cost divided by margin per job.
What goes in a job file?
Quote, photos, receipts and notes.
What if a job seems beyond your skill?
Stop, decline it or refer it to a qualified person or licensed trade.
